question.text:
What is the dimension of the real 3 × 3 matrices whose three row sums are all zero?
(A) 3 (B) 4 (C) 5 (D) 6 (E) 7

solution.text:
Each row has three entries subject to one independent equation, leaving two free entries per
row. Across three rows the dimension is 3 · 2 = 6.

question.text:
What is the dimension of the real 4 × 4 matrices whose row sums and column sums are all zero?
(A) 9 (B) 8 (C) 10 (D) 12 (E) 16

solution.text:
The upper-left 3 × 3 block can be chosen freely. Each remaining entry in the first three rows
or columns is then forced, and the final entry is consistent because total row and column
sums agree. Thus the dimension is 9.

question.text:
What is the dimension of the real vector space of bounded continuous functions on R?
(A) 1
(B) 2
(C) Countably many functions, so it is not a vector space
(D) Infinite
(E) It is not a vector space because sums need not be bounded.

solution.text:
Finite sums and scalar multiples preserve boundedness and continuity. The functions
1, cos x, cos 2x, . . . contain arbitrarily large independent finite lists: integrate a proposed
relation against each cosine on [0, 2π] and use orthogonality. Thus no finite spanning set
exists. Bounded polynomials alone would not establish this on all of R.

question.text:
What is the dimension of the even real polynomials of degree at most 10 satisfying p(1) = 0?
(A) 3 (B) 4 (C) 6 (D) 10 (E) 5

solution.text:
2 4 6 8 10
Even polynomials have basis 1, x , x , x , x , x , of size six. The single nonzero linear
evaluation condition removes one dimension, leaving five.
